title: Let the day perish (Job 3)
hookLine: Job curses the day he was born, and the Bible keeps his words

cards: People say it when someone puts up with a lot: she has the patience of Job. The phrase comes from the letter of James, and it paints a man who suffers quietly, never raising his voice. Hold that picture.
Because after seven days of silence on the ground, Job finally speaks. And the first thing out of his mouth, the opening of the long poem at the heart of the book, isn't patient. It isn't quiet.

teach.h: HE CURSES HIS DAY, NOT GOD
teach.b: Chapter three begins, in the King James Bible: "After this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day." Not God. His day, the day he was born.
"Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived." He wants that day erased, the stars of that night dark, the dawn never to come.
Then the questions: "Why died I not from the womb?" Why is light given to someone in misery? And: "For the thing which I greatly feared is come upon me."
Here's the striking thing about the book's shape. Chapters one and two are prose, like a story.
Right here, with this curse, the book switches to poetry, and stays poetry until the last page. The pain gets the poetry.
And the Bible keeps every word; it doesn't cut this chapter or soften it. The prophet Jeremiah says something close: cursed be the day wherein I was born.
Two people of faith saying the unsayable, and scripture keeps both. Now back to James.
The Greek word translated patience there is hupomone, which the lexicons give as endurance or steadfastness: holding on under a weight without walking away.

teach.h: LET THE DAY PERISH WHEREIN I WAS BORN.
teach.b: That fits Job better than quiet ever did. Job never stops talking to God, even when he's shouting. Christians have often called this kind of speech lament: prayer that tells God the truth about how bad it is.
On this reading, even a curse on your birthday, said to God, is still a way of staying in the conversation.

how: Many Christians pray laments, honest complaints brought to God, using the words of Job, the psalms of lament and Lamentations, and some churches hold services of lament after tragedies.

the patience of Job means he never complained
James's Greek word means endurance. Job complains loudly, but never stops talking to God.

games.q: you've sat in silence for seven days. your friends are waiting. you finally open your mouth. what do you say?
o: curse the day you were born.
games.why: "after this opened Job his mouth, and cursed his day." and the Bible keeps every word of it.

practice: Write, on paper or in your phone, what is actually hard right now, in plain words: angry if you're angry, tired if you're tired, with no lesson tacked on at the end.

If you pray, offer it to God unpolished, the way Job did; if not, let it simply be true on the page. And if what's hard is that you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Hupomone. Greek for endurance, steadfastness that holds on without walking away, the word James really means by Job's patience, even as Job curses the day he was born.

orig.note: Hebrew: let the day perish. the first words of Job's curse in 3:3.

carryVoice: Your line: even this is prayer. Job shouts, but he never leaves. That's four hundred forty-four.
